_about: Why each term is here, in the shape `question`, `why`, `alternatives`, `validated_by`; the question names the questions.json ids it serves.

Relationship.question: What connects to what, over which protocol, and in which order does a flow walk it? (AR1, AR3)
Relationship.why: CALM gives a relationship an id, a protocol, controls and a place in flows. An edge in the graph carries none of those, so the relationship is a node and the plain estate edges (consumes, part_of, runs_in) are derived beside it.
Relationship.alternatives: Edges with attributes: the engine's edges are from, rel, to and nothing else, by design, so every fact about a thing is on a node. A relationship per CALM shape (Connection, Deployment, Composition): rejected, one class with a kind keeps the mapping to CALM one-to-one.

Control.question: Which controls safeguard this node or connection, citing which requirement? (AR2, AR8)
Control.why: A control is the architecture's own statement of what must hold on a path (encryption at rest, no PII), the thing the gates check and the thing an agent must know before it edits.
Control.alternatives: A Policy of the product pack: rejected, a policy is a business obligation; a control is its technical enforcement on a named node, with a requirement schema and a configuration.

Flow.question: What is the sequence of this flow? (AR3)
Flow.why: A flow is the architecture read as a story: which relationship first, which next, which way. Impact of a change is read along it.
Flow.alternatives: A UserJourney of the product pack: rejected, a journey is what a persona does; a flow is what the systems do, over relationships.

FlowStep.question: Which relationship does step N walk, and in which direction? (AR3)
FlowStep.why: A step reifies CALM's transition: a sequence number and a direction on a relationship, which an edge cannot carry.
FlowStep.alternatives: An ordered list attribute on the flow: rejected, a step must be a node to be queried and governed.

NFR.question: Which budgets must this node stay within, and is the measured value inside them? (AR4, AR6)
NFR.why: A requirement with a metric and a budget is the one the architecture is measured against; the product pack's Requirement has neither, and the budget is what arch_context hands an agent.
NFR.alternatives: Attributes on Requirement for every requirement: rejected, most requirements have no metric, and a subclass says which do.

Evidence.question: What measured this requirement, when, and what raised this proposal? (AR6, AR7)
Evidence.why: A measured NFR is a promoted fact only if the measurement is a fact too, with its date and its source; a gate's verdict is evidence the same way.
Evidence.alternatives: A number on the NFR: rejected, a budget is a claim and a measurement is an observation at a date, and the two are different facts.

CodeModule.question: Where is this component implemented, at which path? (AR5, AR9)
CodeModule.why: arch_context takes a path; the walk from a path to a node and its requirements needs the module as a node, and a module nothing traces to is the untraced code H4 reports.
CodeModule.alternatives: The Repository alone: kept, it is coarser; a module is the grain a change touches.

Commit.question: What last changed this module, when, by whom? (AR5)
Commit.why: The graph is compiled on merge; the commit is the link from a fact to the merge that made it true, and from a change proposal to its implementation.
Commit.alternatives: A sha attribute on the module: rejected, one module has many commits and one commit many modules.

ChangeProposal.question: Which changes are proposed, raised by what, about what, settled by which decision? (AR7)
ChangeProposal.why: A gate failure or a budget overrun is the trigger of a change; recording the proposal as a node links trigger, evidence and decision, which the roadmap asks of H5.
ChangeProposal.alternatives: A Decision with status proposed: rejected, a proposal may be rejected and still be worth keeping with what raised it; a decision settles it.

Contract.question: Which contracts does this node consume or expose, at which version, frozen or a draft? (AR10, AR11)
Contract.why: The factory builds contract-first: a frozen contract is what lets a consumer and its provider build in parallel, and a draft one is what makes the consumer wait. The interface alone does not say which; the version does.
Contract.alternatives: A version attribute on Interface: rejected, an interface outlives its versions and two versions are live during a migration; a Contract per version, superseding the last, keeps both facts.

connects_from.question: Where does this relationship start? (AR1)
connects_from.why: CALM's five shapes each have a source side (actor, source node, container); one relation names it for all five, so a walk reads the same whatever the shape.
connects_from.alternatives: Five pairs of relations, one per shape: rejected, five walks for one question.

connects_to.question: Where does this relationship end? (AR1)
connects_to.why: The destination side, one edge per node for the shapes that name several (interacts, deployed-in, composed-of).
connects_to.alternatives: A list attribute of node ids: rejected, edges are how the graph walks.

via.question: Through which interface does the connection go? (AR1)
via.why: CALM's connects names interfaces at either end; the estate already has Interface, so the connection points at it and exposes and consumes are derived.
via.alternatives: Interface ids in metadata: rejected, the interface is a node the estate owns.

offers_option.question: Which options does this relationship offer? (AR1)
offers_option.why: CALM's options shape lists decisions; the product pack has Decision, so each option is one until accepted.
offers_option.alternatives: A class Option: rejected, an option is a decision not yet made.

step_of.question: Which flow is this step in? (AR3)
step_of.why: Exactly one, as CALM's transitions belong to one flow.

over.question: Which relationship does this step walk? (AR3)
over.why: Exactly one, as CALM's transition names one relationship-unique-id.

measurement_of.question: Which requirement is this evidence checked against? (AR6)
measurement_of.why: The measured value and the budget meet here.

evidence_of.question: What is this evidence about? (AR6, AR7)
evidence_of.why: A gate judges a node, a test exercises a connection, a review supports a proposal; the thing judged is named.

implemented_by.question: Where is this component's code? (AR5)
implemented_by.why: Widened from the repository to the module inside it, so a path answers and arch_context can start from one.
implemented_by.alternatives: A new relation implemented_in_module: rejected, one question, one relation.

located_in.question: Which repository holds this module? (AR5)
located_in.why: A module's path is relative to a repository, and the same path may exist in two repositories; naming the repository makes the path an address.

touches.question: Which modules did this commit touch? (AR5)
touches.why: The last change to a module is the commit to read.

prompted_by.question: What raised this proposal? (AR7)
prompted_by.why: The trigger is evidence: a gate verdict or a measurement. Named prompted_by, not triggered_by or raised_by, because the ddd pack declares both with other meanings and the packs compose.
prompted_by.alternatives: triggered_by, raised_by: rejected for the collision.

proposes_change_to.question: What would this proposal change? (AR7)
proposes_change_to.why: Sibling impact is one walk from here along the relationships of the thing changed.

decided_in.question: Which decision settled this proposal? (AR7)
decided_in.why: A proposal ends in a decision, accepted or rejected, recorded as the product pack records every decision.

implemented_in.question: Which commit implemented this proposal? (AR7)
implemented_in.why: The accepted change traces to the merge that made it real.

safeguards.question: What does this control apply to? (AR2, AR8)
safeguards.why: A control's subject is its own relation rather than the estate's `governs` (what a decision shaped), because the gap list, what no control safeguards, is a negation over one relation, and a shared relation would hide an unprotected node behind a decision about it. Named safeguards because the agent pack's guardrails already `protect`.
safeguards.alternatives: Widening `governs` to Control: tried and rejected, AR8 could not be asked.

contract_of.question: Which interface is this contract a version of? (AR10, AR11)
contract_of.why: Exactly one: a contract that spans two interfaces is two contracts.

supersedes.question: Which version replaced which? (AR10, AR11)
supersedes.why: The estate's supersedes, widened to contracts, so a new version retires the old the engine's way, never by overwriting.
supersedes.alternatives: A new relation replaces_version: rejected, one question, one relation.
